name: Wheels Up Experience Inc.

profile.description: Wheels Up Experience Inc. is a U.S. provider of on-demand private aviation, selling membership programs, prepaid Funds, charter, and aircraft management services, and flying members on an owned and operated fleet supplemented by third-party operators. Backed by Delta Air Lines, the company under CEO George Mattson is in the middle of a multi-year fleet modernization from legacy King Air, Citation X and Hawker jets to Embraer Phenom 300 and Bombardier Challenger 300-series aircraft. First-half 2026 revenue was $350.9M (down 4% YoY) and the company continues to report large net losses.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): The main initiative of the last five years is the fleet modernization program, under which Phenom and Challenger revenue more than doubled in Q1 2026 and offset planned declines from legacy jets [1]. This is a restructuring of an existing service rather than a new revenue stream, and total revenue still fell 5% that quarter. AI Deployment (1/2): Management describes the goal as an 'AI-forward' private aviation company and has announced an operations partnership with Palantir, but has reported no quantified AI savings or AI products for customers [4]. Market Share (1/2): Wheels Up is one of the largest U.S. private aviation brands and has a distribution partnership with Delta, but it trails NetJets and Flexjet, and membership revenue fell 31% in 1H 2026 [3]. Pipeline (1/2): The Phenom 300 and Challenger 300 fleet transition has a stated direction but no detailed revenue visibility. R&D (0/1): There is no meaningful R&D spending.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): The stated aim of being 'the most customer-centric, AI-forward and operationally excellent company in private aviation' is generic positioning about how the company will compete, with no larger purpose [4]. Community Impact (1/2): The Wheels Up Cares program (charity flights and causes chosen by members) is a long-running effort, but no dollar amounts are disclosed. Employee Retention (0/2): Repeated executive reshuffles, including the June 2025 go-to-market leadership changes, three CEOs since 2022, and the 2025 sale of non-core services businesses that cut headcount, show an organization still in flux [5][6]. Insider Buying (0/2): There is no evidence of meaningful open-market insider buying. Delta and its co-investors hold control through the 2023 recapitalization.

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: LIQUIDITY FLOOR TRIGGERED: average daily volume of about 105,400 shares at $3.19 equals roughly $336K of daily dollar volume, below the $1M minimum, so Infrastructure is 0 regardless of the other metrics [2]. For reference, the mechanical calculation on the available metrics would have given only about 3/10. Revenue growth of -4% YoY scores 0.53. The 5-year revenue CAGR of about 1.2% ($695M in 2020 to $736.5M in 2025) scores 0.41 at 2x weight [2]. Forward P/E is negative (-0.53) and scores 0. The profit margin of -42% scores 0. D/E and ROE cannot be measured because stockholders' equity is in deficit, and PEG cannot be computed because there are no positive earnings. The Q2 2026 net loss was $107M, or $(2.97) per share [1].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): Flying private jets is a physical, FAA Part 135-regulated service that needs aircraft, certified crews, and maintenance, and AI cannot replace it [1]. The exposure is in the booking and brokerage layer, where AI-driven marketplaces and dynamic pricing tools could commoditize charter sourcing and shrink membership premiums. That is a real risk for a company whose membership revenue fell 31% in 1H 2026 [3]. AI Opportunity (0/1): The Palantir operations partnership is internal tooling, and Wheels Up reports no AI-related revenue [4].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, Wheels Up is still in survival mode. Since the 2023 Delta-led recapitalization, leadership has been focused on stopping losses, selling non-core businesses, and replacing the fleet, not on advancing a lasting cause. There is some willingness to rebuild the model, but frequent leadership turnover and the lack of a purpose beyond 'customer-centric private aviation' make this a finite player trying to reach stability [1][5].

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): The founding idea of making private aviation more accessible through membership was distinctive under founder Kenny Dichter. The current framing, 'customer-centric, AI-forward and operationally excellent' [4], is a set of operating goals, not a vision of a future worth sacrificing for, and it has not been tested across cycles.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): The founder-CEO left in 2023, an interim CEO followed, George Mattson was appointed in 2023, and executive reshuffles continued through June 2025 [5][6]. Asset sales and restructuring reduced headcount. Together these point to an unstable, low-trust environment rather than a Circle of Safety.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management talks about competitors such as NetJets, Flexjet and charter marketplaces in terms of capturing share and improving unit economics. There is no evidence of learning from rivals.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): The company has moved from an asset-light, legacy-fleet membership model to a modernized owned fleet built on Phenom 300 and Challenger 300 aircraft, and has sold non-core services businesses [1]. This is meaningful change, but it was forced by financial distress rather than chosen in service of a cause.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Leadership chose to spend scarce capital on fleet modernization and to exit legacy aircraft and businesses while still losing money (Q2 2026 net loss of $107M), accepting near-term revenue declines in exchange for long-term reliability [1]. One costly long-term bet, made under lender and Delta oversight, earns partial credit.

investment_thesis: The bull case is a turnaround. Wheels Up is replacing a costly, aging mixed fleet with standardized Phenom 300 and Challenger 300 jets, and revenue from that modern fleet more than doubled YoY in Q1 2026 [1]. Gross profit improved by $7M YoY to $9.6M in Q2 2026, and Delta's ownership, distribution partnership and credit support give the company a lifeline most distressed aviation operators lack [1]. If the modern fleet reaches scale and utilization improves, operating leverage could be significant on a market cap of only about $116M [2].
thesis_continued: The bear case is that Wheels Up is still burning cash with no profit in sight. The Q2 2026 net loss was $107M ($2.97/share), 1H 2026 revenue fell 4% to $350.9M, and membership revenue fell 31% [1][3]. Stockholders' equity is in deficit, the forward P/E is negative, and average daily dollar volume of about $336K is below IOWN's $1M liquidity floor, which makes the stock untradeable for the strategy [2]. Equity holders are also exposed to further dilution or restructuring if Delta and the lenders change their stance.
key_catalysts: Fleet modernization reaching scale: Phenom/Challenger revenue more than doubled in Q1 2026; continued retirement of legacy jets could raise gross margin from the Q2 2026 level of $9.6M [1]
Deeper Delta Air Lines commercial integration (corporate travel distribution, SkyMiles linkage) widening the customer funnel [5]
Operating cost reductions from the Palantir-enabled operations platform and the divestiture of non-core services businesses [1][4]
key_risks: Continued heavy losses ($107M Q2 2026 net loss) against a stockholders' deficit, so further dilution or restructuring is a real possibility [1]
Membership revenue down 31% in 1H 2026, which suggests weakening loyalty to the core product versus NetJets, Flexjet and charter marketplaces [3]
Illiquidity: about $336K average daily dollar volume, below IOWN's $1M floor, which makes entry and exit impractical [2]
